issues.explanation: The trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. These cues imply military/combat and sexual-threat or specific geopolitical associations that are not plausibly linked to the reported trauma, and no accompanying threat, appraisal, or strategy items provide a bridge that would make these triggers understandable for this patient. By contrast, the memory items are internally coherent and fit severe reliving after an MVC, as well as the active Memory → Triggers formulation.

'Cars hit by accident' fits the trauma and aligns with the active Memory → Triggers formulation, but 'Sexual situations or intimacy' and 'Arab villages' imply very different trauma contexts (e.g., sexual trauma or combat/terrorism-related threat) that are not represented anywhere else in Memory, Threat, Appraisals, or Strategies. This makes the trigger profile hard to explain as belonging to the same patient and trauma.

For a 51-year-old male welder whose index trauma is a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile clinically with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile. The memory items all concern vivid sensory/bodily reliving of a crash, which coheres with MVC trauma and the active Memory → Triggers edge, but 'Arab villages' implies a war-zone or ethnopolitical context that is not represented anywhere else in the self-report or formulation. This is a clearly implausible trigger for this trauma profile, unlike the crash imagery and alcohol smell triggers, which could plausibly cue MVC memories.

vignette:
Moana, a 51-year-old Māori man who had spent most of his adult life working as a welder, described the beginning of his difficulties as tracing back to a life-threatening motor vehicle collision on his way home from work. He had been driving on a wet stretch of road in the dark when another car crossed into his lane and struck him hard enough to spin his vehicle off the road. In the seconds before impact he remembered the scrape of tires, the jolt of metal, the smell of alcohol on the other driver when bystanders leaned in afterward, and his own body twisted awkwardly against the seatbelt as he struggled to breathe. Since then, those pieces of the event had not stayed in the past. When the memory came back, it did not feel like a story he was telling himself; it came over him as if his body were again trapped in the same position, the pain in the same parts of his body flaring with it, and the whole scene returning with such force that it felt completely real across all his senses at once.

Over time, those memory episodes made the world around him feel charged with danger. Moana found that car sounds could pull him straight into the experience, especially the sudden acceleration of engines or the hiss and grind of traffic near the road outside his house. Seeing cars hit by accident in news footage or even glimpsed on the side of the road would leave him startled and tense, as if he were watching his own crash replayed in front of him. The smell of alcohol was particularly difficult; if he caught it on someone's breath or from a bottle at a family gathering, it could bring the memory sharply to the surface. Because the memory was so vividly bodily and sensory, those cues no longer felt neutral to him. He had come to believe that they were warnings that the danger was not over, but waiting nearby, ready to happen again.

Moana began organizing his days around the hope of not being caught off guard. On his way to the welding shop, he chose longer routes to avoid busy intersections and hesitated at parking lots where cars came and went quickly. At work, the clang of metal and the roar of machinery were familiar enough, but he became increasingly alert whenever vehicles were being moved near the loading bay, scanning for anything that might resemble the crash. He also withdrew from social occasions where alcohol was likely to be present, telling his wife he was tired or had an early shift. At home, he found himself listening for car sounds from the street and stiffening whenever brakes squealed or an engine revved nearby. What frightened him most was that once the memory started, it did not stay contained; it took hold of his body, and then the ordinary things around him - a passing car, a drunk relative at a barbecue, a reported crash on the evening news - seemed to open the door to it again.

As the months passed, these moments came to dominate more of his attention. He became cautious in a way that made practical life smaller, and his marriage felt the strain of the constant adjustments. His wife noticed that he no longer drove unless he had to, and when he did, he sat rigidly with his hands fixed on the wheel, checking mirrors and traffic in a way that left him exhausted before he reached work. At the shop he remained dependable, but he had started avoiding the conversations that used to fill breaks, especially if they drifted toward cars, accidents, or weekend drinking. He was embarrassed by how quickly he could be pulled back into the event, and that shame made him less likely to explain what was happening. By the time he sought help, Moana was exhausted by the effort of staying ahead of the memories and by the fear that one more sound, one more smell of alcohol, or one more image of a smashed car would make the whole thing feel real again. He wanted relief from the bodily return of the crash and the narrowing of his life, but he was most afraid that if he let his guard down, he would be thrown back into that night and lose control all over again.
